bib.title: SCIBENCH: Evaluating College-Level Scientific Problem-Solving Abilities of Large Language Models
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 235

question: How well do LLMs solve open-ended college-level science and math problems, and which problem-solving skills do different prompting strategies improve or hurt?
hypothesis: Existing benchmarks are too easy (high-school level, basic arithmetic, text only), so current LLMs will fall short on college-level problems.
contributions: SCIBENCH: 869 textbook problems (177 multimodal) plus a closed set of 103 exam problems
Benchmarking of open-source and proprietary LLMs under zero-shot, few-shot, CoT and tool-use prompting
LLM-verifier protocol that attributes errors to ten problem-solving skills, giving per-strategy error profiles

method.summary: Free-response college textbook problems with single numeric answers were hand-transcribed to LaTeX; seven unimodal and several multimodal LLMs were run at temperature 0 under zero-shot, CoT, few-shot and Python/Wolfram tool prompts. A GPT-3.5 verifier assigns each wrong answer to one of ten missing skills, spot-checked by humans.
method.task: college-level science/math problem solving with numeric answers

datasets.name: SciBench textbook set
datasets.split: whole set; few-shot examples drawn at random from the same textbook
datasets.source: Halliday fund 142; Engel&Reid thermo 83; Thornton&Marion class 66; Levine quan 41; McQuarrie chemmc 47; Atkins atkins 122; Atkins matter 59; Stewart calc 161; Hogg stat 93; Boyce diff 55. Fair-use selection, academic use only
datasets.preprocessing: PDF to LaTeX via Mathpix, manual annotation by seven people (about 100 examples each), compile-checked; answers stored as float rounded to 3 decimals plus LaTeX plus separate unit; scientific notation split as mantissa and unit; multi-answer problems keep first part or split

datasets.name: SciBench closed exam set
datasets.size: 103 problems per text (Table S1 sums to 104) from 7 exams
datasets.split: Data Mining midterm/final; Machine Learning midterm/final; Differential Equations exam 1, exam 2, final
datasets.source: Midterm and final exams from collegiate CS and Math courses, authorised by instructors
datasets.preprocessing: manually extracted from PDFs into LaTeX to limit leakage into training data; graded by instructor rubrics; mixes free-response, multiple-choice, true-false

inference.samples: 1 run per item, no seeds stated; few-shot examples chosen randomly (shot count not stated in main text)
inference.prompting: System prompt describing categories; zero-shot, zero-shot CoT (two-stage 'Let's think step by step'), few-shot CoT, few-shot Python, few-shot Wolfram. Tool setting only tested few-shot; hand-built verified code in demonstrations

parameters.error_verifier: GPT-3.5 classifies each wrong solution into one of 10 skill categories; humans discard about 20% of incorrect classifications

other.human_baseline: average student scores from course instructor (Data Mining)

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: model answer matches reference within 5% relative tolerance; textbook average weighted by problems per textbook

metrics.name: exam score
metrics.definition: points earned under instructor rubrics out of total points

metrics.name: error-skill share
metrics.definition: share of wrong answers attributed to a missing skill by LLM verifier

eval.protocol: Single run per setting; verifier output checked on 151 samples by two annotators (81.45% correct).

availability.code: repository linked in the paper (URL not given in extracted text); project page https://scibench-ucla.github.io

prompts.text: Please provide a clear and step-by-step solution for a scientific problem in the categories of Chemistry, Physics, or Mathematics. The problem will specify the unit of measurement, which should not be included in the answer. Express the final answer as a decimal number with three digits after the decimal point. Conclude the answer by stating "The answer is therefore \boxed{[ANSWER]}."

Please provide a clear and step-by-step solution for a scientific problem in the categories of Chemistry, Physics, or Mathematics. The problem will specify the unit of measurement. Please translate the solution steps into Python code and encase the Python code within triple backticks for clarity.
Input: [Input-Question] Let's think step by step.

results.setup: GPT-3.5, textbook set, error profile
results.quote: 32.2% and 25.4% error rates in casual ability and logical decomposition ability in the zero-shot CoT setting, respectively, compared to 18.3% and 18.3% in the zero-shot setting

results.quote: with a notable decrease from 14.5% to 6.2%

results.quote: with 46.9% error rate in code conversion skill

results.claim: Wolfram Language does not help few-shot learning.
results.unit: points decrease vs CoT for Claude2
results.setup: Few-shot, Claude2 (6.17 points for LLaMA-2-70B)
results.quote: with a decrease of 6.70% compared to the CoT prompting for Claude2, and a decrease of 6.17% for LLaMA-2-70B

results.claim: The LLM error-skill classifier agrees with human checks 81.45% of the time.
results.setup: 151 sampled classifications across settings checked by two annotators; 123 correct
results.quote: we observed that 123 of them were correctly classified, resulting in an accuracy rate of 81.45%

results.claim: Ten skills were distilled from 112 human error annotations of GPT-3.5.
results.setup: Two college students annotated GPT-3.5 errors on problems with detailed solutions; GPT-4 assisted
results.quote: From 112 such error annotations and with the assistance of GPT-4

results.claim: No prompting strategy wins on all skills.
results.setup: GPT-3.5 error profiles under four settings
results.quote: Our findings suggest that there is a lack of a universally effective setting

limits: Authors argue leakage risk is reduced by hand transcription from PDFs and a closed exam set, but give no contamination test; textbook problems exist in print and solutions manuals may be online.
Textbook set keeps only single-number answers, so it measures numeric final answers, not derivations.
Accuracy uses 5% relative tolerance, which can pass near-miss answers.
Error-skill labels come from a GPT-3.5 verifier, correct on 81.45% of 151 checked; only GPT-3.5 profiles shown in main text.
Exam set is small (103 or 104 problems across 7 exams); exam score figures are inconsistent across the paper (51.57% vs 57.54%).
Single run at temperature 0, no seeds or confidence intervals; models are 2023-era (GPT-4, Claude2, LLaMA-2) and scores have dated.
Multimodal GPT-4 evaluated through captions and OCR, not native vision.
